question: Is 'loud snoring is mostly harmless' a myth?
keyResult: Expert Delphi panel classified 'Although annoying for bed partners, loud snoring is mostly harmless' as a myth: falseness M 4.25 (SD 0.89), public health significance M 4.25 (SD 0.89) on 1-5 scales.

citation.authors: Robbins R, Grandner MA, Buxton OM, et al.
citation.title: Sleep myths: an expert-led study to identify false beliefs about sleep that impinge upon population sleep health practices.

notes: Delphi with 10 experts; ratings are expert opinion, not outcome data. Table 1 read in PMC full text. Conflicts: R.R. (Robbins) has industry consulting in later papers; not declared in this abstract.

question: Is 'alcohol before bed will improve your sleep' a myth?
keyResult: 'Alcohol before bed will improve your sleep' rated a myth: falseness M 4.13 (SD 0.35), public health significance M 4.00 (SD 0.76).

citation.authors: Robbins R, Grandner MA, Buxton OM, et al.
citation.title: Sleep myths: an expert-led study to identify false beliefs about sleep that impinge upon population sleep health practices.

notes: Delphi with 10 experts; ratings are expert opinion, not outcome data. Table 1 read in PMC full text.

question: Is 'watching TV in bed is a good way to relax before sleep' a myth?
keyResult: 'Watching television in bed is a good way to relax before sleep' rated a myth: falseness M 3.50 (SD 0.93), public health significance M 3.14 (SD 1.35).

citation.authors: Robbins R, Grandner MA, Buxton OM, et al.
citation.title: Sleep myths: an expert-led study to identify false beliefs about sleep that impinge upon population sleep health practices.

notes: Delphi with 10 experts; ratings are expert opinion, not outcome data. Table 1 read in PMC full text. Moderate falseness rating: experts were less certain about this one than about snoring or alcohol.

question: Does exercising within 4 hours of bedtime disturb sleep?
keyResult: Experts classified 'Exercising within 4 hours of bedtime will disturb your sleep' as a myth: falseness M 3.25 (SD 1.04), public health significance M 2.43 (SD 0.53).

citation.authors: Robbins R, Grandner MA, Buxton OM, et al.
citation.title: Sleep myths: an expert-led study to identify false beliefs about sleep that impinge upon population sleep health practices.

disagreement: Conflicts with concept no-hard-workouts-right-before-bed and with the 'hard workouts right before bed can keep you up' half of myth-exercise-right-before-bed. Shriane 2023 shift-worker guideline 17 also says nighttime exercise doesn't disrupt sleep for most people. Consider softening the line to 'evening exercise is fine for most people; leave some time to wind down'.
notes: Delphi with 10 experts; ratings are expert opinion, not outcome data. Table 1 read in PMC full text. Lowest-confidence myth in the set (falseness 3.25).

question: Is lying in bed with eyes closed almost as good as sleeping?
keyResult: 'Lying in bed with your eyes closed is almost as good as sleeping' rated a myth: falseness M 4.63 (SD 0.74), public health significance M 3.86 (SD 1.07).

citation.authors: Robbins R, Grandner MA, Buxton OM, et al.
citation.title: Sleep myths: an expert-led study to identify false beliefs about sleep that impinge upon population sleep health practices.

disagreement: Direct conflict with concept rest-even-if-awake ('lying still with your eyes closed still rests your body'). Experts rate the 'almost as good as sleeping' version strongly false. If the concept stays, it should not imply that resting replaces sleep; its value is reducing sleep anxiety, not substituting for sleep.
notes: Delphi with 10 experts; ratings are expert opinion, not outcome data. Table 1 read in PMC full text.

question: Should you stay in bed and keep trying if you can't fall asleep?
keyResult: 'If you have difficulty falling asleep, it is best to stay in bed and try to fall back to sleep' rated a myth: falseness M 4.63 (SD 0.74), public health significance M 3.14 (SD 0.90).

citation.authors: Robbins R, Grandner MA, Buxton OM, et al.
citation.title: Sleep myths: an expert-led study to identify false beliefs about sleep that impinge upon population sleep health practices.

disagreement: Conflicts with concept stay-in-bed-and-breathe ('one expert says to stay in bed and breathe slowly when you wake at night'). The expert panel, stimulus-control evidence, and Shriane 2023 guideline 18 all say get up.
notes: Delphi with 10 experts; ratings are expert opinion, not outcome data. Table 1 read in PMC full text.

question: Is a warmer bedroom better for sleep?
keyResult: 'For sleeping, it is better to have a warmer bedroom than a cooler bedroom' rated a myth: falseness M 3.88 (SD 1.13), public health significance M 2.75 (SD 1.04).

citation.authors: Robbins R, Grandner MA, Buxton OM, et al.
citation.title: Sleep myths: an expert-led study to identify false beliefs about sleep that impinge upon population sleep health practices.

notes: Delphi with 10 experts; ratings are expert opinion, not outcome data. Table 1 read in PMC full text.

question: Can many adults do fine on 5 hours or less, or train themselves to need less sleep?
keyResult: 'Many adults need only 5 or less hours of sleep for general health' rated a myth: falseness M 4.63 (SD 0.52), public health significance M 4.63 (SD 0.74), the highest public health rating of all 20 myths. 'Your brain and body can learn to function just as well with less sleep': falseness M 4.63 (SD 1.06). 'If you can get it, more sleep is always better' was also rated a myth: falseness M 3.25 (SD 1.28).

citation.authors: Robbins R, Grandner MA, Buxton OM, et al.
citation.title: Sleep myths: an expert-led study to identify false beliefs about sleep that impinge upon population sleep health practices.

notes: Delphi with 10 experts; ratings are expert opinion, not outcome data. Table 1 read in PMC full text.

newAdvice: Falling asleep anywhere, any time is a sign you're short on sleep, not a sign of good sleep.
question: Is being able to fall asleep 'anytime, anywhere' a sign of a healthy sleep system?
keyResult: 'Being able to fall asleep "anytime, anywhere" is a sign of a healthy sleep system' rated a myth: falseness M 4.75 (SD 0.46), public health significance M 4.00 (SD 0.93).

citation.authors: Robbins R, Grandner MA, Buxton OM, et al.
citation.title: Sleep myths: an expert-led study to identify false beliefs about sleep that impinge upon population sleep health practices.

notes: Delphi with 10 experts; ratings are expert opinion, not outcome data. Table 1 read in PMC full text. No matching concept in concepts.md.

question: If you have trouble sleeping, is an afternoon nap a good way to make up sleep?
population: general adult public / people with sleep difficulty (expert panel)
keyResult: 'If you are having difficulties sleeping, taking a nap in the afternoon is a good way to get adequate sleep' rated a myth: falseness M 3.13 (SD 1.13), public health significance M 3.14 (SD 1.07).

citation.authors: Robbins R, Grandner MA, Buxton OM, et al.
citation.title: Sleep myths: an expert-led study to identify false beliefs about sleep that impinge upon population sleep health practices.

disagreement: Audience split: for people with insomnia, naps are discouraged; for shift workers (Shriane 2023) and older adults (Li 2023), short naps are recommended or may help. The plain line should not be given as a blanket rule.
notes: Delphi with 10 experts; ratings are expert opinion, not outcome data. Table 1 read in PMC full text.

question: Is sleeping in on weekends a good way to get adequate sleep?
keyResult: 'Sleeping in on weekends is a good way to ensure you get adequate sleep' was NOT classified as a myth: falseness M 2.50 (SD 1.07), public health significance M 3.14 (SD 0.69). The abstract notes this as the lowest falseness rating.

citation.authors: Robbins R, Grandner MA, Buxton OM, et al.
citation.title: Sleep myths: an expert-led study to identify false beliefs about sleep that impinge upon population sleep health practices.

disagreement: Experts did not agree that weekend catch-up is false. The current myth line ('doesn't fully make up') is more cautious and probably fine, but should not be phrased as a strong myth.
notes: Delphi with 10 experts; ratings are expert opinion, not outcome data. Table 1 read in PMC full text. Same table lists 'sleeping with a pet is comforting and improves sleep quality' as not a myth (falseness 2.63).

newAdvice: Hitting snooze for a short while is fine for most people; it isn't the sleep-wrecker it's made out to be.
question: Is hitting snooze worse than getting up at the first alarm?
keyResult: Experts classified 'Hitting the snooze when you wake up is better than getting up when the alarm first goes off' as a myth: falseness M 3.75 (SD 1.04), public health significance M 2.75 (SD 1.04).

citation.authors: Robbins R, Grandner MA, Buxton OM, et al.
citation.title: Sleep myths: an expert-led study to identify false beliefs about sleep that impinge upon population sleep health practices.

disagreement: Expert opinion (Robbins 2019) conflicts with later experimental data (Sundelin 2024) that found 30 minutes of snoozing cost about 6 minutes of sleep with no clear harm. Recommend not adding an anti-snooze rule.
notes: Delphi with 10 experts; ratings are expert opinion, not outcome data. Table 1 read in PMC full text.

newAdvice: Hitting snooze for a short while is fine for most people; it isn't the sleep-wrecker it's made out to be.
question: Does snoozing harm sleep, cognition or mood?
population: habitual snoozers, adults (lab study n = 31; survey n = 1732)
keyResult: Survey of 1732 respondents: snoozing is widespread, especially in younger people and later chronotypes. In a within-subject lab study of 31 habitual snoozers, 30 min of snoozing improved or did not affect cognitive test performance on rising versus abrupt awakening; snoozing cost about 6 min of sleep and prevented awakenings from slow-wave sleep (N3); no clear effects on cortisol awakening response, morning sleepiness, mood, or overnight sleep architecture.

citation.authors: Sundelin T, Landry S, Axelsson J
citation.title: Is snoozing losing? Why intermittent morning alarms are used and how they affect sleep, cognition, cortisol, and mood.

disagreement: Contradicts the Robbins 2019 expert rating of the snooze myth.
notes: Small lab sample of habitual snoozers only; within-subject crossover, not a long-term trial.

question: Are late weekend bedtimes and wake times harmless for teens if they get enough sleep?
population: adolescents (expert panel) and US parents/caregivers of adolescents (n = 200)
keyResult: Ten adolescent sleep myths identified by 12 experts. Most prevalent among parents: 'Going to bed and waking up late on the weekends is no big deal for adolescents, as long as they get enough sleep during that time' (74% of parents/caregivers); experts rated its falseness M 3.8 (SD 1.0), public health significance M 4.2 (SD 0.9).

citation.authors: Robbins R, Beebe DW, Byars KC, et al.
citation.title: Adolescent sleep myths: Identifying false beliefs that impact adolescent sleep and well-being.

notes: Expert opinion plus a 200-person parent survey. Table read in PMC full text.

newAdvice: Melatonin is not automatically safe for children and teens just because it's natural; ask a clinician before using it.
question: Is melatonin safe for adolescents because it is natural?
keyResult: 'Melatonin supplements are safe for adolescents because they are natural' was endorsed by 66% of parents/caregivers; experts rated falseness M 4.0 (SD 0.7), public health significance M 4.0 (SD 0.9).

citation.authors: Robbins R, Beebe DW, Byars KC, et al.
citation.title: Adolescent sleep myths: Identifying false beliefs that impact adolescent sleep and well-being.

disagreement: Concept melatonin-for-jet-lag-or-shifts is written for adults; it should not be read as advice for children or teens.
notes: Audience-specific. The AASM 2022 health advisory on melatonin in children (PMID 36239049) was located but has no abstract and its text was not in the PMC XML, so it was not read.

newAdvice: Teens' body clocks run later; support later school start times rather than blaming teens for sleeping late.
question: Do later school start times help teens sleep more, or do teens just stay up later?
keyResult: 'If school starts later, adolescents will stay up that much later' was endorsed by 69% of parents/caregivers; experts rated falseness M 4.1 (SD 0.9), public health significance M 4.6 (SD 0.7). Experts also rated 'If adolescents can't get up for school, they are lazy' (4.4) and 'An adolescent's sleep schedule is largely out of their control' (4.3) as false.

citation.authors: Robbins R, Beebe DW, Byars KC, et al.
citation.title: Adolescent sleep myths: Identifying false beliefs that impact adolescent sleep and well-being.

notes: Expert opinion; see Cochrane 2017 and Wang 2026 for outcome data.

newAdvice: Teens' body clocks run later; support later school start times rather than blaming teens for sleeping late.
question: Do later school start times improve sleep and well-being in high school students?
keyResult: 11 unique studies with 297,994 participants. Quality of evidence very low. Six studies reported significant positive relationships between later school start times and amount of sleep; academic outcomes, absenteeism and alertness were mixed. Authors could not determine effects with any confidence.

citation.authors: Marx R, Tanner-Smith EE, Davison CM, et al.
citation.title: Later school start times for supporting the education, health, and well-being of high school students.

notes: COI declared: three review authors evaluated one of the included Toronto studies (did not extract its data). Policy-level advice; individuals can't change it alone.

newAdvice: Teens' body clocks run later; support later school start times rather than blaming teens for sleeping late.
question: How much do delayed school start times change teen sleep duration and depression?
keyResult: Six studies included. Delayed school start time was associated with an average increase in sleep duration of 69 min (SMD 0.63, moderate effect); depressive symptoms (five studies) pooled SMD -0.20 (small). High heterogeneity in both analyses.

citation.authors: Wang RC, Lee MI, Aroul GS, et al.
citation.title: Delayed school start times to improve sleep duration and mitigate depression in adolescents: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

notes: Only six studies, mostly observational. Authors declare no competing interests.

question: How much sleep do children, teens, adults and older adults need?
keyResult: Recommended: 14-17 hours for newborns, 12-15 hours for infants, 11-14 hours for toddlers, 10-13 hours for preschoolers, 9-11 hours for school-aged children, 8-10 hours for teenagers; 7 to 9 hours for young adults and adults; 7-8 hours for older adults.

citation.authors: Hirshkowitz M, Whiton K, Albert SM, et al.
citation.title: National Sleep Foundation's updated sleep duration recommendations: final report.

disagreement: The plain line ('Most adults need 7 to 9 hours') is adult-only. Children and teens need more; the NSF range for older adults is 7-8 hours. Variable text per audience is needed.
notes: Expert consensus (RAND/UCLA). Not free to read per OpenAlex. AASM pediatric consensus (Paruthi 2016, PMID 27250809, PMC4877308) exists but its abstract gives no numbers.

question: Does a nightly bedtime routine help young children sleep?
keyResult: Narrative review and conceptual model: a nightly bedtime routine is presented as promoting healthy sleep plus language, literacy, emotional and behavioural regulation, attachment and family functioning. Components include nutrition (feeding, healthy snack), hygiene (bathing, oral care), communication (reading, singing) and physical contact (massage, cuddling).

citation.authors: Mindell JA, Williamson AA
citation.title: Benefits of a bedtime routine in young children: Sleep, development, and beyond.

notes: Narrative (not systematic) review. COI: Mindell has consulted for and received grants from Johnson & Johnson Consumer Inc. (declared as not related to this paper). Children only; strongest evidence base for routines is in young children.

question: Does screen use impair sleep across the lifespan?
keyResult: NSF 16-person panel (modified Delphi). Consensus on 5 of 10 statements: (1) in general, screen use impairs sleep health among children and adolescents; (2) the content of screen use before sleep impairs sleep health of children and adolescents; (3) behavioural strategies and interventions may attenuate the negative effects. No consensus was reported for adults in the abstract.

citation.authors: Hartstein LE, Mathew GM, Reichenberger DA, et al.
citation.title: The impact of screen use on sleep health across the lifespan: A National Sleep Foundation consensus statement.

disagreement: Evidence for harm is clear in children and teens and unsettled in adults, so the 'keep phones out of children's bedrooms' half of the plain line is better supported than the adult half.
notes: Authors declare no conflicts. Probably also covered by the screens area; included here for the audience split.

newAdvice: Put babies to sleep on their back, on a firm, flat surface, in your room but not in your bed.
question: What sleep environment reduces sleep-related infant deaths?
keyResult: AAP policy: about 3500 US infants die of sleep-related deaths each year. Recommends supine positioning; a firm, noninclined sleep surface; room sharing without bed sharing; avoiding soft bedding and overheating; plus human milk feeding, avoiding nicotine, alcohol, marijuana, opioids and illicit drugs, routine immunization and pacifier use.

citation.authors: Moon RY, Carlin RF, Hand I, et al.
citation.title: Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations for Reducing Infant Deaths in the Sleep Environment.

disagreement: Bed-sharing is normal in many cultures, and some breastfeeding advocates disagree with a blanket 'no bed-sharing' rule; AAP includes guidance for assessing specific bed-sharing situations. Adult co-sleeping advice must never be applied to infants.
notes: Infants only. US guideline. Not free to read per OpenAlex.

newAdvice: Put babies to sleep on their back, on a firm, flat surface, in your room but not in your bed.
question: Is bed sharing with an infant linked to SIDS?
keyResult: Eleven studies. Combined OR for SIDS in all bed-sharing versus non-bed-sharing infants 2.89 (95% CI 1.99-4.18). Highest risk for infants of smoking mothers (OR 6.27; 95% CI 3.94-9.99) and infants <12 weeks old (OR 10.37; 95% CI 4.44-24.21).

citation.authors: Vennemann MM, Hense HW, Bajanowski T, et al.
citation.title: Bed sharing and the risk of sudden infant death syndrome: can we resolve the debate?

notes: Older than 2015 but a landmark meta-analysis; case-control data. Not free per OpenAlex.

newAdvice: From about 28 weeks of pregnancy, go to sleep on your side (left or right), not on your back.
question: Is going to sleep on your back in late pregnancy linked to stillbirth, and does left vs right side matter?
keyResult: IPD meta-analysis of case-control studies (cases n = 851; controls n = 2257). Supine going-to-sleep position associated with increased odds of late stillbirth (aOR 2.63, 95% CI 1.72-4.04) compared with left side. Right side had similar odds to left (aOR 1.04, 95% CI 0.83-1.31). Population attributable risk for supine going-to-sleep position 5.8% (3.2-9.2).

citation.authors: Cronin RS, Li M, Thompson JMD, et al.
citation.title: An Individual Participant Data Meta-analysis of Maternal Going-to-Sleep Position, Interactions with Fetal Vulnerability, and the Risk of Late Stillbirth.

disagreement: 'Sleep on your LEFT side' is a common version of this advice; the data show either side is equally fine. Does not relate to concept left-side-for-reflux.
notes: Case-control data (recall bias possible). Pregnancy only, from 28 weeks.

newAdvice: From about 28 weeks of pregnancy, go to sleep on your side (left or right), not on your back.
question: Is sleep position up to 30 weeks of pregnancy linked to adverse outcomes?
keyResult: No association between non-left lateral or supine sleep at the first visit (aOR 1.00 [95% CI 0.89-1.14]) or third visit (aOR 0.99 [95% CI 0.89-1.11]) and the composite of stillbirth, small-for-gestational-age or gestational hypertensive disorders. Objectively measured supine sleep >=50% of the time was not linked to the composite outcome.

citation.authors: Silver RM, Hunter S, Reddy UM, et al.
citation.title: Prospective Evaluation of Maternal Sleep Position Through 30 Weeks of Gestation and Adverse Pregnancy Outcomes.

disagreement: Prospective data up to 30 weeks show no association; case-control data (Cronin 2019) show risk from 28 weeks. Advice should be limited to late pregnancy and should not alarm women who wake on their back.
notes: COI: one author received research funds from Kyndermed; one receives UpToDate royalties. Only up to 30 weeks.

question: Is habitual daytime napping linked to health outcomes, and does duration matter?
keyResult: Habitual napping increased risk of all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease, metabolic disease and cancer, and decreased risk of cognitive impairment and sarcopenia. Naps of 30 min or longer were linked to higher risk of all-cause mortality, CVD and metabolic disease; naps under 30 min showed no significant risks. Authors suggest shortening naps to 30 min or less.

citation.authors: Yang YB, Zheng YB, Sun J, et al.
citation.title: To nap or not? Evidence from a meta-analysis of cohort studies of habitual daytime napping and health outcomes.

notes: Observational; long naps may be a marker of illness rather than a cause. Many cohorts from napping cultures (e.g. China). Authors declare no conflicts. Not free per OpenAlex.

question: Does daytime napping help or harm cognition in older adults?
keyResult: 35 studies (23 observational, 12 intervention). Possible inverted U-shaped association: short and moderate naps benefited cognitive health compared with no napping and long napping. One session of afternoon napping might improve psychomotor function and working memory, with some inconsistency.

citation.authors: Li J, McPhillips MV, Deng Z, et al.
citation.title: Daytime Napping and Cognitive Health in Older Adults: A Systematic Review.
citation.journal: J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci

disagreement: For older adults the message is 'keep naps short', not 'avoid naps'.
notes: COI: one author consulted for Merck. Older adults only.

question: Is a long siesta linked to worse night sleep in young adults?
keyResult: Cross-sectional regression: longer siesta duration was a risk factor for poor sleep quality. Sleep position, the interval between lunch and the siesta, and sleepiness 30 min after the siesta mediated the relationship.

citation.authors: Wang H, Li J, Han Y, et al.
citation.title: Siesta characteristics mediated the association between siesta duration and sleep quality in Chinese incoming college freshmen.

notes: Cross-sectional (studyType 'cohort' is the closest option). Siesta-culture population; shows napping advice should be framed as 'keep it short' in cultures where a midday nap is normal.

newAdvice: Older adults: sleeping pills usually help only a little and raise the risk of falls and confusion; try other approaches first.
question: Do the benefits of sedative hypnotics outweigh the risks in people over 60 with insomnia?
keyResult: 24 RCTs (2417 participants). With sedatives: sleep quality improved (effect size 0.14), total sleep time increased (mean 25.2 minutes), night awakenings decreased (0.63). Adverse cognitive events 4.78 times more common (95% CI 1.47 to 15.47), adverse psychomotor events 2.61 times more common (1.12 to 6.09), daytime fatigue 3.82 times more common (1.88 to 7.80) than placebo.

citation.authors: Glass J, Lanctôt KL, Herrmann N, et al.
citation.title: Sedative hypnotics in older people with insomnia: meta-analysis of risks and benefits.

disagreement: Overlaps with check-your-medicines but is a distinct audience-specific message.
notes: Pre-2015 landmark meta-analysis; newer drug classes (e.g. orexin antagonists) not covered.

question: Does scheduled bright light improve insomnia in older adults?
population: older adults with primary insomnia (n = 51, aged 63.6 ± 7.1)
keyResult: 12-week program of sleep hygiene plus 45 min daily bright (~4,000 lux) or dim (~65 lux) light, morning or evening. Subjective and objective sleep changes after bright light were not significantly different from dim light, though light shifted circadian phase predictably.

citation.authors: Friedman L, Zeitzer JM, Kushida C, et al.
citation.title: Scheduled bright light for treatment of insomnia in older adults.

disagreement: Bright light for early waking in older adults is often suggested but this RCT found no benefit over dim light.
notes: Small sample; pre-2015.

question: Does CBT-I help menopausal women with insomnia and hot flashes?
population: perimenopausal and postmenopausal women aged 40-65 with insomnia and hot flashes (n = 106)
keyResult: At 8 weeks ISI scores decreased 9.9 points with telephone CBT-I vs 4.7 with menopause education, between-group difference 5.2 points; PSQI between-group difference 2.7 points. At 8 and 24 weeks, 70% and 84% of CBT-I participants were in the no-insomnia range vs 24% and 43% of controls. Hot flash frequency did not differ, but hot flash interference fell more with CBT-I.

citation.authors: McCurry SM, Guthrie KA, Morin CM, et al.
citation.title: Telephone-Based Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia in Perimenopausal and Postmenopausal Women With Vasomotor Symptoms: A MsFLASH Randomized Clinical Trial.

notes: Single-site US trial. A Cochrane review on CBT-I in perimenopause is registered (protocol PMID 42029175) but not yet published.

question: Does CBT-I work for people with insomnia plus depression, PTSD or other mental disorders?
population: adults with insomnia and a comorbid mental disorder (22 RCTs)
keyResult: Effect sizes for insomnia severity reduction: 0.5 (CI 0.3-0.8) depression, 1.5 (CI 1.0-1.9) PTSD, 1.4 (CI 0.9-1.9) alcohol dependency, 1.2 (CI 0.8-1.7) psychosis/bipolar, 0.8 (CI 0.1-1.6) mixed. Comorbid symptom reduction post-treatment: 0.5 (CI 0.1-0.8) depression, 1.3 (CI 0.6-1.9) PTSD; no significant effects on comorbid symptoms at follow-up.

citation.authors: Hertenstein E, Trinca E, Wunderlin M, et al.
citation.title: Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia in patients with mental disorders and comorbid insomnia: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

disagreement: Confirms CBT-I advice applies to people with depression or anxiety too; it should not be withheld because of a mental-health condition.
notes: Authors declare no conflicts. Note: sleep restriction within CBT-I needs care in bipolar disorder (not stated in this abstract; general clinical caution).

question: Do digital sleep programs help college students and young adults?
population: college students and young adults aged 18-25 (13 RCTs, 5251 participants)
keyResult: Digital interventions (CBT-I, mindfulness, sleep education via web or app) improved sleep quality (Hedges g=-1.25), sleep efficiency (g=0.62), insomnia severity (g=-4.08), dysfunctional beliefs (g=-1.54), sleep hygiene (g=-0.19) and sleep knowledge. Evidence certainty moderate to very low; very high heterogeneity (I2 up to 99%).

citation.authors: Lu YA, Lin HC, Tsai PS
citation.title: Effects of Digital Sleep Interventions on Sleep Among College Students and Young Adults: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

notes: Implausibly large pooled effect for insomnia severity (g=-4.08) with I2=99%; treat cautiously. No conflicts declared.

question: How well does sleep hygiene education alone treat insomnia?
keyResult: Sleep hygiene education improved ISI from pre- to post-treatment (MD 3.4, 95% CI 2.08-4.64) but was inferior to CBT-I (MD 3.8), partial CBT-I (MD 4.5), exercise (MD 2.9) and acupressure (MD 1.9). 85.71% of trials had high risk of bias.

citation.authors: Ruan JY, Liu Q, Chung KF, et al.
citation.title: Effects of sleep hygiene education for insomnia: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

disagreement: Important framing for the whole dataset: tip lists (sleep hygiene) are weaker than CBT-I for people with insomnia. Supports pointing people with lasting insomnia to cbt-for-insomnia rather than more tips.
notes: No conflicts declared.

newAdvice: If trying hard to fall asleep keeps you awake, stop trying: let yourself lie quietly awake instead.
question: Does paradoxical intention (giving up the effort to sleep) help insomnia?
keyResult: Compared with passive comparators, paradoxical intention led to large improvements in key insomnia symptoms and large reductions in sleep-related performance anxiety; versus active comparators the improvements were smaller but still moderate for several central outcomes. Methodologically stronger studies are needed.

citation.authors: Jansson-Fröjmark M, Alfonsson S, Bohman B, et al.
citation.title: Paradoxical intention for insomnia: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

disagreement: Related to rest-even-if-awake and stay-in-bed-and-breathe, but different: the point is dropping sleep effort, not resting as a substitute for sleep. Can sit alongside get-up-if-you-cant-sleep (both reduce performance anxiety).
notes: Insomnia patients only; few, older trials.

question: What sleep advice should shift workers get, and how does it differ from standard sleep hygiene?
keyResult: 84% of experts agreed tailored guidelines were needed for shift workers. 18 consensus guidelines, including: aim for 7-9 hours per 24 hours, possibly split into a main sleep plus shorter sleeps; a sleep schedule per shift type; sleep somewhere cool (16-20ºC/60-68ºF), dark and quiet; wear sunglasses driving home after night shift; caffeine can help before and during a shift; avoid nicotine entirely or within 6 hours of bed; limit food on night shifts; regular exercise, noting that nighttime exercise doesn't disrupt sleep for most people.

citation.authors: Shriane AE, Rigney G, Ferguson SA, et al.
citation.title: Healthy sleep practices for shift workers: consensus sleep hygiene guidelines using a Delphi methodology.

disagreement: Several general concepts must not be given to shift workers as written: keep-naps-short-and-early, keep-a-regular-sleep-schedule, get-up-at-the-same-time, get-morning-daylight (after a night shift, morning light should be blocked), caffeine-cutoff.
notes: Expert consensus; effectiveness not yet tested (authors say so). Guideline table read in PMC full text.

question: Should shift workers nap?
keyResult: Guideline 6: 'Use napping as a helpful tool.' Short naps (15-20 minutes) can boost alertness; longer naps (90 minutes) can reduce sleep debt; naps under 15 min may be too short; naps over 20 min raise sleep-inertia risk; avoid longer naps in the 4-6 hours before main sleep. The abstract notes that current guidelines may contradict fatigue-management advice, e.g. advising against daytime napping.

citation.authors: Shriane AE, Rigney G, Ferguson SA, et al.
citation.title: Healthy sleep practices for shift workers: consensus sleep hygiene guidelines using a Delphi methodology.

disagreement: Direct audience exception to keep-naps-short-and-early ('before mid-afternoon'). For shift workers, naps are a recommended tool and timing follows the roster.
notes: Expert consensus.

question: Do planned naps during night shifts reduce sleepiness?
keyResult: Most investigators found that, despite short periods of sleep inertia right after naps, night-shift napping led to decreased sleepiness and improved sleep-related performance. No study examined workplace safety outcomes.

citation.authors: Ruggiero JS, Redeker NS
citation.title: Effects of napping on sleepiness and sleep-related performance deficits in night-shift workers: a systematic review.

disagreement: Supports the shift-worker exception to keep-naps-short-and-early.
notes: Small samples, mixed designs. Narrative synthesis.

question: Do sleep interventions help rotating night shift workers?
population: rotating night shift workers (30 studies; 25 in meta-analysis)
keyResult: Interventions grouped as pharmacological (n = 7), light therapy (n = 9), cognitive behavioural (n = 7), aroma or alternative therapy (n = 4) and shift schedule modification (n = 3). Overall mean effect size moderate (Hedges' g = 0.59; 95% CI 0.33-0.84).

citation.authors: Jeon BM, Kim SH, Shin SH
citation.title: Effectiveness of sleep interventions for rotating night shift workers: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

notes: Pools very different interventions; abstract does not report per-type effects.

newAdvice: Avoid smoking or vaping in the hours before bed; if you quit, sleep may be rough for a few weeks before it improves.
question: Is nicotine use linked to poorer sleep, and what happens to sleep after quitting?
keyResult: Sleep alterations appear to persist for the first few weeks of withdrawal and predict relapse. Without NRT, N1 sleep fell in those abstinent for 6 months, while REM sleep fell only in those who relapsed. One study found long-term nicotine patches were associated with an increase in slow-wave sleep vs short-acting patches. Limited evidence suggests sleep restoration with NRT.

citation.authors: Mauries S, Rolland B, Mallevays M, et al.
citation.title: Conditions of sleep restoration after smoking cessation: A systematic review.

notes: Heterogeneous results. Gap: Irish 2015 and Shriane 2023 both list nicotine as a sleep hygiene item; no concept covers it. Plain line needs care so it never discourages quitting.

newAdvice: Avoid smoking or vaping in the hours before bed; if you quit, sleep may be rough for a few weeks before it improves.
question: Is e-cigarette use linked to shorter or worse sleep?
population: e-cigarette users, adults and adolescents (14 cross-sectional studies)
keyResult: E-cigarette users had higher odds of shorter sleep duration than non-users (pooled OR 1.38, 95% CI 1.24-1.55). Several studies reported higher odds of insomnia and sleep-medication use. Among adolescents, e-cigarette use was associated with a 33 to 61% increased risk of inadequate sleep.

citation.authors: Sulthana H, Jan A, Verma A, et al.
citation.title: Impact of electronic cigarette use and sleep duration, sleep issues and insomnia: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

notes: All cross-sectional; cannot show causation. No conflicts declared.

newAdvice: Avoid smoking or vaping in the hours before bed; if you quit, sleep may be rough for a few weeks before it improves.
question: What is the evidence behind common sleep hygiene recommendations for the general public?
keyResult: Review of sleep hygiene recommendations on exercise, stress management, noise, sleep timing, and avoiding caffeine, nicotine, alcohol and daytime napping. Epidemiologic and experimental research generally supported an association between individual recommendations and nocturnal sleep, but direct effects of individual recommendations remain largely untested in the general population.

citation.authors: Irish LA, Kline CE, Gunn HE, et al.
citation.title: The role of sleep hygiene in promoting public health: A review of empirical evidence.

disagreement: Gap check: of Irish's eight areas, nicotine is the only one without a concept. Exercise, stress, noise, timing, caffeine, alcohol and napping are all covered.
notes: Narrative review; abstract does not give per-item effect sizes.

question: Which sleep hygiene recommendations does a 2023 clinical review list?
keyResult: Recommendations: 7 to 9 h of sleep, a consistent sleep/wake schedule, a regular bedtime routine, regular exercise, a contemplative practice, and avoiding caffeine, alcohol, heavy meals and light exposure later in the day.

citation.authors: Baranwal N, Yu PK, Siegel NS
citation.title: Sleep physiology, pathophysiology, and sleep hygiene.

disagreement: Gap check: every recommendation in this abstract already has a concept (get-enough-sleep-for-you, keep-a-regular-sleep-schedule, have-a-wind-down-routine, exercise-regularly, try-a-guided-meditation/relaxation-techniques, caffeine-and-big-meals-early, no-alcohol-close-to-bedtime, less-bright-light-in-the-evening). No new advice.
notes: Narrative review; no conflicts declared. Not free per OpenAlex.

newAdvice: A pet in the bedroom is usually fine; if it wakes you, keep it off the bed.
question: Does a dog in the bedroom or on the bed disturb human sleep?
population: healthy adults with dogs (n = 40, 88% women), 7 nights actigraphy
keyResult: Mean actigraphy: 475±101 minutes in bed, 404±99 minutes total sleep, 81%±7% sleep efficiency. Human sleep efficiency was lower when the dog was on the bed than when it was only in the room (P=.003). Authors conclude a dog in the bedroom may not be disruptive.

citation.authors: Patel SI, Miller BW, Kosiorek HE, et al.
citation.title: The Effect of Dogs on Human Sleep in the Home Sleep Environment.

notes: Small, single-dog households, no comparison group without dogs. Not free per OpenAlex. Robbins 2019 experts did not classify 'sleeping with a pet improves sleep quality' as a myth (falseness 2.63).

newAdvice: A pet in the bedroom is usually fine; if it wakes you, keep it off the bed.
question: Does co-sleeping with pets affect children's and teens' sleep?
keyResult: 34.6% co-slept with a pet sometimes or frequently. Sleep profiles were largely identical across never, sometimes and frequent co-sleepers on subjective (child, parent) and objective (PSG, actigraphy) measures. Frequent co-sleepers had the highest subjective sleep quality but the longest PSG onset latency compared with the sometimes group.

citation.authors: Rowe H, Jarrin DC, Noel NAO, et al.
citation.title: The curious incident of the dog in the nighttime: The effects of pet-human co-sleeping and bedsharing on sleep dimensions of children and adolescents.

notes: Cross-sectional comparison; adolescents only.

question: Does treating a snorer's sleep apnea improve the bed partner's sleep?
population: 10 married couples (male patients with suspected OSA and their spouses)
keyResult: Patients' median AHI fell from 26 to 7 on CPAP. Spouses' median arousal index fell from 21 to 12 (P < .01) and median sleep efficiency rose from 74% to 87% (P < .01). Authors estimate this equals an additional 62 minutes of sleep per night for spouses.

citation.authors: Beninati W, Harris CD, Herold DL, et al.
citation.title: The effect of snoring and obstructive sleep apnea on the sleep quality of bed partners.

disagreement: Supports adding the partner angle to snoring advice: a snoring partner's sleep apnea also costs the other person sleep.
notes: Very small, single-night, pre-2015. Not free per OpenAlex.

newAdvice: Sharing a bed with a partner doesn't harm sleep for most couples; if a partner's snoring or movement wakes you, get the snoring checked or try separate beds.
question: How does sharing a bed with a partner affect sleep?
population: young healthy heterosexual couples (sleep lab PSG)
keyResult: Compared with sleeping alone, co-sleeping was associated with about 10% more REM sleep, less fragmented REM (p = 0.008), longer undisturbed REM fragments (p = 0.0006) and more limb movements (p = 0.007). No other sleep stages changed significantly. Partners' sleep stages were more synchronised during co-sleep.

citation.authors: Drews HJ, Wallot S, Brysch P, et al.
citation.title: Bed-Sharing in Couples Is Associated With Increased and Stabilized REM Sleep and Sleep-Stage Synchronization.

notes: Small lab study of young healthy couples; sample size not given in abstract. 'Separate beds' half of the line has no direct trial evidence found.

newAdvice: Be wary of sleep advice from popular videos and influencers; much of it is sponsored or wrong. Check it against a health service or sleep society.
question: How accurate are popular YouTube videos about sleep?
population: popular YouTube sleep/insomnia videos vs expert-led videos
keyResult: Most popular videos averaged 8.2 (± 2.2) million views; expert-led videos 0.3 (± 0.2) million. Commercial bias in 66.7% of popular videos and 0% of expert videos (P < .012). Popular videos featured more misinformation than expert videos (P < .001).

citation.authors: Robbins R, Epstein LJ, Iyer JM, et al.
citation.title: Examining understandability, information quality, and presence of misinformation in popular YouTube videos on sleep compared to expert-led videos.

notes: COI declared: R.R. consulted for Savoir Beds, Oura Ring and others; S.F.Q. for Jazz Pharmaceuticals and others; L.J.E. for AASM and others. Small number of videos.

newAdvice: Be wary of sleep advice from popular videos and influencers; much of it is sponsored or wrong. Check it against a health service or sleep society.
question: How reliable is insomnia advice on TikTok?
keyResult: Only 20 videos (15.7%) had high educational value and 11 (8.7%) moderate. Only 5 videos scored highest for consistency with guidelines, 5 recommended seeing a physician, and 2 included scientific references. About 55% of physicians' videos had GQS ≥ 3, versus 25%, 18% and 0% for other health professionals, general users and brand accounts. Quality did not correlate with engagement; sponsored videos had lower quality.

citation.authors: Papadopoulou S, Karkala A, Engelshove E, et al.
citation.title: When sleep advice goes viral: medical reliability of insomnia content on TikTok.

notes: Cross-sectional content analysis; no conflicts declared.

newAdvice: Be wary of sleep advice from popular videos and influencers; much of it is sponsored or wrong. Check it against a health service or sleep society.
question: How common are sleep myths in the US public, and are they linked to behaviour?
keyResult: 10 of the 20 expert-identified myths were endorsed by at least 50% of respondents. Higher myth scores were associated with more inconsistent bedtimes (OR 1.07 [1.04-1.09]), more frequent napping (OR 1.11 [1.09-1.14]), more in-bed activities (β = 0.35), behaviours incompatible with sleep hygiene (β = 0.24) and perceiving fewer consequences of insufficient sleep (β = -0.13).

citation.authors: Pantesco EJ, Kan IP
citation.title: False beliefs about sleep and their associations with sleep-related behavior.

notes: Cross-sectional; uses the Robbins 2019 myth list. Not free per OpenAlex. No conflicts declared.

question: Is mouth taping during sleep safe and effective?
population: people with mouth breathing, sleep-disordered breathing or OSA (10 studies, 213 patients)
keyResult: 10 studies, 213 patients. Two showed statistically significant improvement in AHI or oxygen desaturations; others showed no difference and discussed potential risks including asphyxiation with nasal obstruction. Authors conclude there is a potentially serious risk of harm for individuals indiscriminately practising the trend.

citation.authors: Rhee J, Iansavitchene A, Mannala S, et al.
citation.title: Breaking social media fads and uncovering the safety and efficacy of mouth taping in patients with mouth breathing, sleep disordered breathing, or obstructive sleep apnea: A systematic review.

disagreement: Supports the current cautious line; could be firmer: don't tape your mouth if your nose is blocked or you may have sleep apnea.
notes: Many included studies excluded people with nasal obstruction. No conflicts declared.

question: What does the evidence say about TikTok claims for mouth taping?
keyResult: Nine studies met criteria: two found improvements in OSA metrics (one with taping alone, one with taping plus a mandibular advancement device); one non-OSA study reported less snoring with taping plus other measures; one asthma study found no benefit. Most common TikTok claims were improved sleep and oral health; few have been tested.

citation.authors: Fangmeyer SK, Badger CD, Thakkar PG
citation.title: Nocturnal mouth-taping and social media: A scoping review of the evidence.

notes: Scoping review; heterogeneous evidence.

question: Does nasal obstruction or mouth taping change sleep apnea measures?
population: adults with induced or post-surgical nasal obstruction; 2 mouth-taping studies
keyResult: Nasal obstruction was associated with an increase in AHI (+13.78 events/h) and ODI (+7.45 events/h). Two mouth-taping studies (narrative only) found reduced AHI in mild OSA; no meta-analysis possible for taping.

citation.authors: Alshehri NA, Alsaif NF, Abdulrazaq AN, et al.
citation.title: Impact of Nasal Obstruction and Mouth Taping on Sleep Apnea Indicators: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

notes: Supports nose breathing in general; mouth-taping evidence is two small studies. No conflicts declared.

newAdvice: Use a sleep tracker lightly, if at all; it can't diagnose sleep problems, and if checking the numbers makes you worry about sleep, stop.
question: Can consumer sleep trackers be used to diagnose or treat sleep disorders?
keyResult: AASM position: because of lack of validation and FDA clearance, consumer sleep technologies cannot be used for diagnosis and/or treatment of sleep disorders at this time, but may enhance the patient-clinician interaction when presented in the context of an appropriate clinical evaluation.

citation.authors: Khosla S, Deak MC, Gault D, et al.
citation.title: Consumer Sleep Technology: An American Academy of Sleep Medicine Position Statement.

notes: 2018; devices have improved since. NSF issued a 2026 position statement (PMID 41792005) whose abstract is non-specific and whose authors include industry employees (Samsung, Verily, Meta, Variowell founder).

newAdvice: Use a sleep tracker lightly, if at all; it can't diagnose sleep problems, and if checking the numbers makes you worry about sleep, stop.
question: Can sleep tracker data drive a perfectionistic, anxious pursuit of ideal sleep ('orthosomnia')?
population: patients seeking treatment based on sleep-tracker data (case reports)
keyResult: Describes a growing number of patients seeking treatment for self-diagnosed insufficient sleep or insomnia based on tracker data; the tracker data may drive a perfectionistic quest for ideal sleep, and patients often trust tracker data over validated tests.

citation.authors: Baron KG, Abbott S, Jao N, et al.
citation.title: Orthosomnia: Are Some Patients Taking the Quantified Self Too Far?

disagreement: Ojalvo 2023 found no worsening of sleep worry with a tracker in insomnia patients.
notes: Case reports only; coined the term.

newAdvice: Use a sleep tracker lightly, if at all; it can't diagnose sleep problems, and if checking the numbers makes you worry about sleep, stop.
question: Do wrist sleep trackers worsen sleep worry in people with insomnia?
population: primary-care insomnia patients (Fitbit n = 14, diary n = 12)
keyResult: Sleep quality, sleep reactivity to stress and quality of life improved in all patients over 4 weeks with no significant differences between the Fitbit and diary groups. Authors conclude wearables do not necessarily exacerbate sleep worry in insomnia.

citation.authors: Ojalvo D, Pacheco AP, Benedict C
citation.title: A useful tool or a new challenge? Hand-wrist-worn sleep trackers in patients with insomnia.

disagreement: Tempers the orthosomnia concern: harm is not universal.
notes: Very small; groups differed at baseline; allocation method not stated in abstract (studyType RCT may overstate).

question: Is device-measured weekend catch-up sleep linked to mortality or heart disease?
population: UK adults with wrist accelerometers (n = 73,513; 8.0 years follow-up)
keyResult: Weekend catch-up sleep was not associated with mortality (≥ 2 hours group: HR 1.17 [95% CI 0.97 to 1.41]) or incident CVD (HR 1.05 [0.94 to 1.18]); results held in adults sleeping under 6 hours on weekdays.

citation.authors: Chaput JP, Biswas RK, Ahmadi M, et al.
citation.title: Device-measured weekend catch-up sleep, mortality, and cardiovascular disease incidence in adults.

disagreement: Consistent with the myth line (catch-up does not make up for short weekday sleep): no protective benefit found. Earlier self-report studies suggested a benefit.
notes: Observational, UK Biobank-type cohort.
